--- a/paper/main.tex

-Running a new language model on every benchmark is costly, yet leaderboards hold many earlier scores. We ask which $k$ benchmarks to run on a new model so that its remaining scores can be inferred, and how large $k$ must be. We study factor-model prediction with greedy Bayesian A-optimal selection (it minimises the average posterior variance of the unrun scores) under a protocol that holds out whole model families, fits before selecting, and uses paired, family-clustered intervals, on dense blocks of MTEB and HELM MMLU results and on MTEB matrices with missing cells. Three benchmarks close 81--96\% of the gap between the column-mean predictor and a leave-one-benchmark-out predictor, but 90\% needs one benchmark on HELM MMLU and nine or more on MTEB, with wide intervals. Greedy selection beats random selection by 6--11\% of the error, mostly at $k\le3$, and meets our pre-specified 10\% margin on one pool of three; with missing cells (21--70\% observed) it closes 0.71--0.80 of the gap at $k=3$, against 0.55--0.74 for random. Later and stronger models are predicted worse and too low. A closed-form risk is exact with known parameters and gives the shape of the error-versus-$k$ curve, but its level is 36--69\% off on real data.
